question: The Digital Markets Act1 mandates that gatekeeping search engines share data with their competitors (Article 6(11)). While data sharing may potentially lead to fair competition, significant concerns have arisen regarding the privacy implications of such data transfers.

Building trust in the data sharing process requires effective anonymisation practices and a thorough understanding of the potential privacy risks involved. Specific details regarding the anonymisation methods and oversight mechanisms employed to ensure that the anonymised data cannot be re-identified remain unclear. In the light of this: 1.
How exactly did the Commission evaluate potential privacy risks stemming from mandatory data sharing on such a large scale?
What measures has it taken to ensure the effectiveness of the anonymisation techniques used?
What oversight mechanisms will be put in place to verify the techniques’ effectiveness?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.6.2024) The Commission’s enforcement of the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1 concerning data sharing, such as ranking, query, click and view data in relation to search, is framed by Article 6 (11), requiring that personal data must be anonymised before it can be shared.

The DMA clarifies that the relevant data is considered anonymised if personal data is irreversibly altered so that information does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or where the data subject is not or no longer identifiable. In this process, the quality and usefulness of the data must not be substantially degraded.

Under the DMA, gatekeepers are responsible for ensuring effective compliance with these obligations. It is for gatekeepers to ensure the protection of personal data, including against possible re-identification risks. The Commission assesses whether gatekeepers’ solutions comply with all the requirements of Article 6(11).
The Commission remains in contact with stakeholders, gatekeepers, and potential beneficiaries to monitor the effectiveness of the implemented compliance solution including the anonymisation approach.

The Commission cooperates with the High-Level Group for the DMA, which is the forum to ensure coherence and effective complementarity in the implementation of the DMA and of other sectoral regulations applicable to designated gatekeepers; the European Data Protection Board is one of the members of this High-Level Group.

The Commission has instruments that it can use to carry out its monitoring duties, including requesting information from the gatekeepers and/or third parties, and appointing independent experts. The Commission will not hesitate to use all available instruments at its disposal to ensure effective compliance by gatekeepers.
